title: Man shot by police was troubled but had good heart, mom says
article: The man killed by police during a Kitchener robbery this week had struggled for years with depression and drug addiction.

Trevor Colin Graham, 26, was shot once in the chest after he was confronted by two Waterloo regional police officers Tuesday night while fleeing the Shoppers Drug Mart store in the Sunrise Centre with stolen prescription drugs.
His mother, Karyn Graham, said in an interview yesterday that he had a difficult life marked by mental illness, addiction and minor run-ins with the law.
"He was certainly loved and he had a good heart," she said. "He was just very troubled with moods."
Despite his problems, Karyn Graham said his death is baffling because he seemed to be in good spirits and determined to turn his life around just hours before the fatal shooting.

She also said there is nothing to speculation that her son may have been responsible for previous robberies in the area -- including an armed holdup at the same drugstore six days earlier -- because he was in a Brantford jail until Nov. 17. He had been in custody since August after breaching the terms of an eight-month conditional sentence for being an accessory to a coffee shop robbery in Brantford.
Trevor Graham was originally from the Hamilton area.
He came to stay with his mother and her boyfriend in Kitchener after she picked him up from jail, where he had recently earned a high school diploma.
"He was hoping that was going to give him a new start," said Karyn Graham. "We spent a lot of time talking and he was very focused on being successful at a career."
A close friend, Vicki Chiasson of Brantford, also said Trevor Graham was released from jail just three days before the shooting and couldn't have been involved in the previous robberies.
A police spokesperson, however, did not rule out a possible link between the night of the shooting and a rash of earlier incidents on the west side of the city.
"Our investigators are looking at the other robberies," said Insp. Bryan Larkin.
"It's very premature and we're not in a position to speak publicly in relation to what other people are telling The Record."
The shooting is being investigated by a civilian agency that examines all police incidents in Ontario resulting in death or serious injury.
The Special Investigations Unit typically releases few details until its probe into possible police wrongdoing is finished.

In this case, it's not known if Graham was armed or what happened during a brief exchange with the two uniformed officers before he was shot in a vestibule at the front entrance of the Ottawa Street South store.
Karyn Graham said her son got hooked on a painkiller called OxyContin after he had it prescribed for a back injury several years ago.
But she said he had done extremely well in a methadone treatment program for opiate addicts and showed no signs of drug abuse before his death.
Chiasson also said she is convinced he wasn't strung out on drugs or seeking them for his own use when he committed the robbery.
"They destroyed his life initially and he worked hard to get off them," she said. "Never in the whole time I knew him did he even think about going down that road again."
Just two hours before the shooting, Karyn Graham said, she took her son to a home improvement store to buy drywalling supplies for renovations at the Kitchener house where he was staying.
"He had all the tools ready for the next morning," she said.
When they got home, Karyn Graham said, he told her he was going for a walk to "clear his head" and buy some potato chips at a nearby store.
The next thing she heard, he had been killed while fleeing the drugstore with stolen prescription drugs.

She is pleased with the way the civilian agency is handling the case, but said she has a lot of questions because her son wasn't a violent, hardened criminal with a history of offences involving weapons.
Her theory is that he was after drugs he knew he could easily sell on the street because he was broke after leaving jail.
"Why wouldn't they allow him to come out, wait for backup, if they felt he was armed?" she asked. "They should not have confronted him like that."
Trevor Graham got married in 2002 to a woman in Liverpool, England, whom he met chatting online.
His wife came here to live, Karyn Graham said, but returned to England about two years later when his depression and mood swings got worse. They didn't have any children.
The family had tried since childhood to get him help, but he was never formally diagnosed or stabilized for long.
He excelled during a year at a private, military-style boarding school near Welland as a teenager -- at a cost of $26,000 -- and considered joining the army.
But when he started getting into minor trouble with the law as a teen, Karyn Graham said, the justice system couldn't deal with his complex needs.

"The courts should be working along with willing parents," she said. "Instead of putting him in jail at the expense of the public, if we had just been able to get him the right treatment, we'd have been happy to do that."

Trevor Graham checked himself into a psychiatric facility two years ago, his mother said, but his "cry for help" went unheeded after he was jailed for missing an appointment with his probation officer.
With a high school diploma and some construction experience under his belt, he was hoping to train as a heavy equipment operator when he got out of custody for the last time.
There was also talk of a possible reunion with his wife.
"He had goals and he was doing it - struggling, but doing it," said his mother. "He struggled all his life."
Trevor Graham is also survived by his father, Colin, and brother Adam, 22.
Visitation is scheduled for Saturday in Waterdown, near Hamilton. At his request, there won't be a funeral.
